answer.evidence: The clearly trained first-layer units fall into three groups. (1) Units 3, 8, 21, 24, 27 and 28 have broad positive weights over the central region (rows ~4-19, cols ~5-18). These units carry the largest weights in the tensor (99 at r10c15 in unit 8, at r15c10 in unit 24 and at r15c13 in unit 27; 98 in units 8, 27 and 28). They all feed layer-2 unit u1 positively (71, 40, 73, 62, 76, 99), and u1 has an output weight of +88. (2) Units 2, 14, 16, 18, 19, 20, 25 and 30 are negative in the centre and positive in a broad periphery. For example, unit 2 has -90/-89/-88 near the centre and +96/+93/+92 at the edges. These units mostly feed u1 negatively. Together the two groups form a centre-minus-surround nodule contrast pathway. (3) Units 1, 6, 9, 11, 12, 13, 15, 17, 23 and 31 have diffusely negative weights over the whole image. I found no compact cluster of strong, same-sign weights at an edge or corner that is shared across units and differs from these centre and ring patterns. Two candidates looked tentative at first: the right edge around rows 9-12, cols 22-23 (unit 16 and others) and the lower-right area around rows 15-17, cols 19-22. Both are either inconsistent in sign across units, part of the broad periphery and centre patterns, or not significant when averaged over all 32 units. Units 0, 4, 10 and 22 look essentially untrained, with weights within the initialization range of about ±80.
answer.main_feature: The model scores how bright and large the central nodule is against its surroundings. Central positive detectors minus a peripheral ring feed layer-2 unit u1 and unit u13, and both push toward malignant; diffuse dark-lung units contribute toward benign.
